clue.text: Put to shame for having a go

parts.note: to have a go is to have a bash, an attempt

explanation.surface: Someone is humiliated for daring to make an attempt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having a go' is read as 'having a bash', so the go gives BASH after the A.
explanation.definitionFit: To abash someone is to embarrass or disconcert them.

clue.text: Exhausted artist had dinner outside

indicators.note: the dining word sits outside, wrapping round the artist

parts.note: had dinner means dined
RA, Royal Academician, is the usual abbreviation for an artist

explanation.surface: A painter, worn out, has eaten his meal out of doors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' seems to say the meal was eaten alfresco, but it is the container signal; RA (Royal Academician) is the standard crossword artist.
explanation.definitionFit: Drained is a common idiom for utterly tired, with all energy used up.

clue.text: House that can think out loud!

indicators.note: said out loud, the word for think becomes a different word of the same sound

parts.note: to muse is to think or ponder

explanation.surface: A building is credited with the power of thought, voiced aloud.
explanation.walkthrough: Mews are rows of converted stables, a common kind of British town house; the exclamation mark flags the pun on muse.
explanation.definitionFit: A mews is a row of dwellings converted from stables, so a mews can be a residence.

clue.text: Collapsed stand gave a number of benefits

indicators.note: a collapsed structure falls into a jumble, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A grandstand fell down and brought about some good outcomes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collapsed' rearranges STAND GAVE A.
explanation.definitionFit: Advantages are plural benefits or favourable points, hence a number of them.

clue.text: Actors' posture corrected

definitions.note: the possessive stands in for the plural groups that actors belong to; the def reads loosely as companies of players

indicators.note: a corrected posture is put right, so the letters are put into a new order

explanation.surface: Performers have their bearing put right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'corrected' rearranges POSTURE; the definition is the apostrophised plural, taken as companies of actors.
explanation.definitionFit: A troupe is a touring company of performers, so several of them are bands of players.

clue.text: In the theatre, expect to see growth

indicators.note: the letters are found inside the words theatre and expect running together

explanation.surface: At the playhouse you can count on some development.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' points at the letters straddling the end of 'theatre' and the start of 'expect'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tree is a plant that has grown, a woody growth from the ground.

clue.text: Demand something to follow apple pie

definitions.meaning: to demand is to command or instruct
apple-pie ... is the idiom for perfect neatness, so the word comes after apple pie

explanation.walkthrough: 'apple-pie order' means everything perfectly arranged; the surface pretends to talk about dessert courses.
explanation.definitionFit: To order is to command; and the phrase apple-pie order completes the familiar idiom for tidiness.

clue.text: Worry the skipper? Turbulence is partly responsible

indicators.note: only part of these words is responsible for the answer, so it lies inside them

explanation.surface: The captain is anxious that rough air is partly to blame.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the join of 'skipper' and 'Turbulence'.
explanation.definitionFit: To perturb someone is to disturb or unsettle them.

clue.text: Plant rush before spring

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece comes before, above, the second

parts.note: to rush is to speed
a spring is a well, a source of water

explanation.surface: Hurry ahead of the arrival of the new season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spring' suggests the season but is a water source.
explanation.definitionFit: Speedwell is a small blue-flowered herb, Veronica.

clue.text: Who killed the Simpson boy and got the drinks?

definitions.text: Who killed the Simpson boy and got the drinks?

parts.note: Bart is the son in the cartoon family The Simpsons
one who ends something, a finisher, is an ender

explanation.surface: A murder mystery: who did away with the cartoon lad and then served the drinks?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines a drinks server while also building BART plus ENDER, someone who finishes Bart off.
explanation.definitionFit: A bartender serves drinks behind a bar.

clue.text: Back the last cockney nag

parts.note: the last part of something is its end

indicators.note: Cockney speech famously drops initial aitches

parts.note: a nag is an old horse

explanation.surface: Put money on the final, East End racehorse.
explanation.walkthrough: A Cockney is a working-class Londoner whose accent drops the H, so 'cockney nag' is 'orse.
explanation.definitionFit: To endorse a candidate or idea is to support it.

clue.text: Trim mould around joints

indicators.note: the moulding word goes around the joints

parts.note: to mould is to shape
hips are joints of the body

explanation.surface: Cut back the mould growing round the joints of meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trim' looks like a verb but is the adjective meaning neat.
explanation.definitionFit: Trim and shipshape both describe something neat and in good order.

clue.text: Good drinks reduced to powder

parts.note: a round is one set of drinks bought for a group

explanation.surface: Fine drinks were milled into a fine dust.
explanation.walkthrough: A round of drinks is what one person buys for everyone in the group, a pub custom.
explanation.definitionFit: Coffee beans that are ground have been crushed into tiny particles.

clue.text: Teacher's expression of disapproval to alternative

definitions.note: read as Teacher is, the 's linking to the wordplay

parts.note: tut is the sound made in disapproval
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: A schoolteacher clicks the tongue disapprovingly at a different option.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of 'Teacher's' is read as 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A tutor is a private teacher or instructor.

clue.text: Split career

definitions.meaning: a split is a rip in fabric
to career is to rush along headlong

explanation.walkthrough: 'career' is the verb meaning to hurtle, not a profession; the two senses are pronounced differently.
explanation.definitionFit: A rip in cloth and a headlong dash share one spelling, with different pronunciations.

clue.text: Hula-hoop expert at the circus?

parts.note: someone skilled with a hoop could whimsically be called a master of rings, but the big-top official is meant

explanation.walkthrough: The circus official in charge of the ring is whimsically pictured as a person expert in spinning hoops.
explanation.definitionFit: The ringmaster is the presenter who directs circus performances in the ring.

clue.text: Obscure confectionary product

definitions.meaning: to obscure an issue is to blur or evade it
a soft sweet made of sugar, butter and milk

explanation.walkthrough: 'Obscure' is a verb here, to fudge an issue, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: To blur an issue deliberately and a soft creamy sweet share one name.

clue.text: Roofer cut off part of garage

indicators.note: off means wrong or awry, so these letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A tiler sliced away a section of the car workshop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' rearranges ROOFER CUT.
explanation.definitionFit: The forecourt is the open area in front of a filling station where the pumps stand.

clue.text: Base one? Good lord

parts.note: the Roman numeral I is one
a lord is a noble

explanation.surface: Is this a low person? Good heavens!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good lord' looks like an exclamation but gives G and NOBLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Base and ignoble both mean dishonourable or mean-spirited.

clue.text: Sleeps when the bridge is up

indicators.note: in a down clue going up reads the word from bottom to top

parts.note: a span is a bridge or the arch of one

explanation.surface: People doze off whenever the drawbridge is raised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is up' reads SPAN backwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Naps are short sleeps or dozes.

clue.text: Win, without a drink!

indicators.note: without means the following letter is left out

parts.note: to win is to gain

explanation.surface: Victory, and nothing to drink!
explanation.walkthrough: 'without a' takes the A out of GAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Gin is a juniper-flavoured spirit.

clue.text: The case of rogue inspector's regret?

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outside, its first and last letters

parts.note: Inspector Morse is a fictional Oxford detective

explanation.surface: A detective sorrowfully considers the case of a villain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case' looks like a police case but means the outside of 'rogue'; Inspector Morse is a British TV detective.
explanation.definitionFit: Remorse is deep regret or guilt for wrongdoing.

clue.text: Pitman and a student for Beryl, perhaps

parts.note: a pitman works down a pit, a coal miner
L, for learner, stands for a student, as on British L-plates

explanation.surface: A collier and a pupil stand in for a woman named Beryl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beryl' looks like a woman's name but is a gemstone; L for learner comes from the L-plates on British learner drivers' cars.
explanation.definitionFit: Beryl is a crystalline gemstone, an example of a naturally occurring rock substance.

clue.text: Shell's product line primarily fruit

parts.note: a pear is a fruit

indicators.note: primarily means first, so take the opening letter of line

explanation.surface: An oil company's output is mostly fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shell' suggests the oil company but means an oyster's shell.
explanation.definitionFit: An oyster produces a pearl inside its shell.

clue.text: A second dimension to first of several judges

parts.note: size is a dimension or measurement

indicators.note: first of picks the opening letter of several

explanation.surface: A further measurement is offered to the leading figure among some judges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' simply joins the pieces in order.
explanation.definitionFit: The assizes were former English courts presided over by travelling judges, so loosely the judicial sittings.

clue.text: Add an extra note for oil deposits

parts.note: to add up is to sum
PS, postscript, is an extra note at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: Append a further message about oil reserves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'note' suggests music but is a written note.
explanation.definitionFit: Sumps are reservoirs where engine oil collects.

clue.text: Jack perhaps came across an inaccurate rumour

indicators.note: the card word comes across, around, the other piece

parts.note: a jack is an example of a playing card

explanation.surface: A man called Jack heard some false gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' looks like a man's name but is a playing card.
explanation.definitionFit: A canard is an unfounded story or false report.

clue.text: Game played with mat on the outskirts of bury

indicators.note: in a down clue on means placed above the next piece

parts.note: a rug is a mat

indicators.note: the outskirts of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A sport played on a mat at the edge of a northern town.
explanation.walkthrough: Bury is a town in Lancashire, but here only its first and last letters count.
explanation.definitionFit: Rugby is a team ball sport, named after the school where it began.

clue.text: Joins in raising commotion

indicators.note: raising in a down clue reads the word from the bottom upwards

parts.note: to kick up a stink is to cause a commotion

explanation.surface: Someone takes part in stirring up trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raising' reads STINK upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To knit is to unite or bond, as broken bones knit.

clue.text: Bob's final couple spell "idée fixe"

indicators.note: the final couple of letters of Bob's name, ignoring the possessive

parts.note: a spell is a period, a session

explanation.surface: Bob's last pair cast a magic charm on a fixed idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spell' suggests magic but is a stretch of time.
explanation.definitionFit: An idée fixe is a fixed idea that dominates the mind, a fixation.

clue.text: German open tasked the outright leaders

indicators.note: leaders are the first letters of the following words

explanation.surface: A German tennis open asked the outright champions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaders' picks the first letters of 'open tasked the outright'.
explanation.definitionFit: Otto is a typical German male name.

clue.text: Location? Listen to sense

indicators.note: listening means the word is heard rather than read, giving a same-sounding word

parts.note: sight is one of the five senses

explanation.surface: Where is it? Pay attention to good sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sense' suggests reason but is one of the five senses.
explanation.definitionFit: A site is a place or position where something stands.

clue.text: Honourable and leading wing of the Tories

parts.note: to be up is to be ahead, leading
the Conservatives, the British Tories, sit on the political right

explanation.surface: An upstanding and prominent figure in the Conservative party.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tories are the British Conservative Party, on the right of politics.
explanation.definitionFit: An upright person is morally sound and decent.

clue.text: Should it make one patient?

parts.note: patient seems to mean calm, but as a noun it is someone under medical care

explanation.walkthrough: 'patient' looks like the adjective for calm but means a person receiving medical care.
explanation.definitionFit: Medical care is what turns someone into a patient.

clue.text: Cry, though in the pink

parts.note: in the pink suggests good health, but hunting pink is the red coat worn by foxhunters, whose shout is meant

explanation.walkthrough: 'in the pink' sounds like being healthy, but 'hunting pink' is the red coat worn by British foxhunters, who give this shout on sighting a fox.
explanation.definitionFit: Tally-ho is the huntsman's call on sighting the fox.
